column1: What is the project description you receive called, in the lecture's terms?
column2: Just an idea, or "one seed" - a starting point, not a specification.

column1: From the project description, in which direction do you build the rationale?
column2: Upwards, to the bigger picture.

column1: From the project description, in which direction do you build the justification?
column2: Downwards, to available resources and feasibility.

column1: Which of the three artefacts sits closest to the client's own description?
column2: The purpose.

column1: What is the rule about deciding the product?
column2: Do not directly jump to what needs to be built; stay at the rationale level until fully convinced.

column1: Define rationale (Canvas wording).
column2: The broader context and underlying need that gives rise to the project.

column1: What two questions generate a rationale?
column2: So what? and "Who cares?"

column1: What does the "So what?" question ask?
column2: What difference is it going to make, and why is it important to build this project.

column1: What does the "Who cares?" question ask?
column2: Who the project will help or affect - the ultimate beneficiaries.

column1: Give four categories of beneficiary named in the lecture.
column2: Environment, people, community, and industry.

column1: Can "so what" and "who cares" points be separated into fixed positions in the list?
column2: No. They can be placed at any position; there is no definite position for either.

column1: What must a high-level rationale bullet point never mention?
column2: The product or the solution.

column1: How must rationale bullet points be ordered?
column2: High level to low level, with each point feeding into the next.

column1: How long should each rationale bullet point be?
column2: One sentence, roughly one line.

column1: Roughly how many rationale bullet points were suggested?
column2: Around 8 to 10.

column1: In the ice-cap melting example, what was the top of the rationale ladder?
column2: The planet and climate change, with global warming as a cause.

column1: What proved the read-out rationale example was written correctly?
column2: The product description was never revealed, yet the ladder still worked - it never touched the product.

column1: Define purpose (Canvas wording).
column2: The specific goal or intent of the project within that larger context.

column1: What relationship does the purpose assert?
column2: The relationship between the high-level rationale (the why) and the product the client wants built.

column1: Why can't a purpose claim to solve the high-level problem?
column2: Because the product contributes only a small part; it cannot be a large-scale solution to the whole problem.

column1: What two components make up a well-formed purpose statement?
column2: What is built, plus what it contributes to.

column1: Define justification (Canvas wording).
column2: Why this solution is feasible and valuable, often referring to evidence, demand, or practicality.

column1: What is justification assessed against?
column2: Available resources - team, budget, time - in communication with the client.

column1: What is justification also known as?
column2: The business case for the project.

column1: Can competitor products serve as justification evidence?
column2: Yes. If a similar solution has worked for competitors, that supports feasibility.

column1: Define what a client "says".
column2: Their literal words or the written description - vague and under-specified.

column1: Define what a client "wants".
column2: Their initial expectation: what they are picturing but have not fully explained.

column1: Define what a client "needs".
column2: The real business requirement, once resources, cost and limitations are applied.

column1: Why do says, wants and needs differ?
column2: Unclear communication, evolving understanding, and unspoken assumptions.

column1: What does the endpoint of the says-to-needs journey become in Scrum?
column2: The product backlog.

column1: When can says, wants and needs coincide?
column2: When the client is technical enough.

column1: If says, wants and needs coincide, what do you still do?
column2: Carry out the discussions anyway, to confirm rather than assume.

column1: In the fitness studio example, what did the client say?
column2: We need a calendar where users can book a class with one click.

column1: Name two operational needs in the fitness studio example that the client never mentioned.
column2: Preventing double bookings and managing class capacity (also payment integration, waitlisting).

column1: What is the diagnostic tell for a "says" statement?
column2: It is quoted, or is a description of the solution in vague terms.

column1: What is the diagnostic tell for a "wants" statement?
column2: Language like "envision" or "imagine" - what they picture after discussion.

column1: What is the diagnostic tell for a "needs" statement?
column2: It emerges from analysis or user research, not from what was stated.

column1: What is "the first core question" to ask a client?
column2: Why - why does this matter, and who are the affected parties.

column1: What are the two benefits of asking the client "why"?
column2: It gives you more detail about the project, and it signals to the client that you are more interested in developing it.

column1: What must you do before meeting the client?
column2: Your homework: infer and write down a candidate rationale, and prepare a sequence of questions.

column1: Is research required for the initial project rationale?
column2: No. It must be based on current knowledge and team discussion only.

column1: What learning analogy was used to justify questioning the client?
column2: A class where students who do not ask questions do not learn; you are now on the other side of that.

column1: Where do non-technical clients' project descriptions usually come from?
column2: A reference software product they have seen - a competitor's or a colleague's.

column1: What question exposes a reference-product origin?
column2: Is this description your own idea, or is it coming from somewhere else?

column1: What conflict arises from a reference-product description?
column2: The inherited technology stack may not suit the core functionalities requested.

column1: What do you do when the client's suggested technology doesn't fit the functionality?
column2: Counter-question: put it to the client that those technologies are not the best for implementing those functionalities.

column1: What does a product owner do?
column2: Acts as a representative of the client, monitoring project development and carrying communication between client and team.

column1: In this course's projects, what is the relationship between client and product owner?
column2: They are the same person.

column1: What test applies to words like "scalable" and "accessible"?
column2: Each and every word must have a meaning clear in your mind for this specific project.

column1: What does "scalable" mean in the food-sharing justification?
column2: That it can scale in future if there are more users.

column1: What were the three faults in the first AI-generated rationale?
column2: Not in bullet points, not one-liners, and it talked about the project or solution.

column1: Which rationale fault persisted even after the AI was told to skip implementation detail?
column2: It still talked about the project itself, just not the implementation.

column1: What happened to the AI rationale when "proper flow" was enforced?
column2: The top of the ladder rose from "pollinators like bees are vital" to "a healthy planet depends on stability of ecosystems and biodiversity".

column1: What does the flow correction teach about checking your own rationale?
column2: Enforcing flow reveals whether your top point is genuinely the highest level, or whether there is a level above it.

column1: What is the ownership rule for AI-assisted work?
column2: You must own what you submit; you cannot attribute it to the AI and disclaim responsibility.

column1: How do you satisfy the ownership rule in practice?
column2: Read the output fully and justify it in your own mind before submitting.

column1: Which two Canvas module topics were NOT covered in this lecture?
column2: Agile, and Scrum and Kanban - both deferred to the following week.
